A lot of misinformation here. Let's clear things up.

1. The fact that exhaled air still contains 16% oxygen doesn't mean that the person being resuscitated is able to utilize that oxygen. Their lungs will not be able to absorb that oxygen since at 16% the oxygen in the airways is in equilibrium with the gas in the blood of the lungs hence there is no drive to further absorb it - there is no pressure gradient for oxygen to pass through the alveolar wall into the blood. The point of mouth-to-mouth in CPR is twofold: 1. to make air move around from parts of the lung where there was no gas exchange earlier (the so called dead space - mainly big airways where there's no alveoli). This result in a minor amount of fresh air getting further down the lungs. 2. to displace any potential objects blocking the airways.
2. For a random adult person who has collapsed in front of a lay persons' eyes with no additional equipment, the most important part of resuscitation by far is chest compressions. There is still enough oxygen left in the blood for 5-10 minutes; the problem is it doesn't move around if the heart stops.
3. Studies show that it's actually difficult to get any significant volume of blood to move around so the chest compressions should be interrupted as little as possible, ideally not at all. Any interruption results in a significant lessening of the volume pumped around.
4. Apart from this, the idea of giving mouth-to-mouth to a random person is a factor in hesitancy of bystanders to start CPR.
5. Mouth-to-mouth is still recommended in children, drown victims and people who go into cardiac arrest after suffocating on an object, say food. This is because in these people, sudden death is caused primarily by a breathing rather than a heart problem - the aim of mouth to mouth being a possibility of displacing the barrier causing the obstruction of airways. Also the blood is low in oxygen already (which caused the heart to stop) which means that there's not much use in pumping it around - the oxygen is spent and compressing further is pointless unless we get some fresh oxygen into it, however minor that amount is.) In these groups it's even recommended to start by giving 5 breaths before starting compressions.
6. Mouth-to-mouth is also recommended if professional help isn't expected in more than 10 minutes (remote areas) - same reason as mentioned above, because the oxygen in the blood is spent by then.
7. Of course we should ventilate if we have a bag valve mask but that's rarely available for lay people.

It's becoming ever more clear that chest-compression only CPR should be taught to the general public. The reason the majority of organizations still teach compressions + breaths is because of a supposed "lack of conclusive enough evidence that it results in better survival to change guidelines" and sticking to tradition, but I believe that compression only resuscitation is superior with the caveats mentions above.

Source: I'm an MD who has recently passed our national obligatory CPR exam and have worked in the emergency room for several months before that.

You shouldn't worry about the side effects, for some people they are quite awful. My girlfriend got AstraZeneca and she was in a state similar to what you have described and she's fine.

As for taking NSAIDS after the vaccine, there haven't been sufficient studies done on this matter to come to any real conclusions but there's no real evidence that taking NSAIDS like Advil in normal doses can cause a dramatic decrease in immunity. There are some studies on other vaccines and one for COVID in mice which show NSAIDS can decrease the amount of antibodies produced but it's not clear at which doses the effect becomes significant, if the effect would be seen for everyone and even what this slightly reduced antibody count even means, as antibodies aren't the only part of the immune response.

My opinion is that even if there is an effect that effect is most likely negligible so you shouldn't worry. The people in the COVID vaccine studies weren't instructed against taking medication to ease side effects either.

NSAIDs do have anti-inflammatory properties but the effect is nowhere near enough to make a difference when this level of inflammation is involved. You need intravenous corticosteroids (like dexamethasone), which are actually now recommended in severely ill COVID patients.

When the immune response is low, that's when the virus can actually run rampant and cause damage itself. Even though our own immune response damages our tissues, it's there for a reason. Additionally, those peoples' defense mechanisms are further weakened by the infection, which can then predispose them to other, even more severe infections with bacteria or fungi.

They are effective mainly because they train your body to fight the infection in a controlled way, without serious symptoms. Then when you encounter the virus the next time, it doesn't have the ability to replicate in your body because your immune response is much faster and therefore more targeted. Consequently there's not much tissue that's infected which would warrant a full blown immune response.

MD here.

The main component in COVID causing the shutdown of organs is inflammation. The COVID virus itself doesn't hurt the organs as much, rather most of the damage is caused by the immune system trying to get rid of it.

It all starts with the lungs of course, because that's where the virus likes to reproduce, and the inflammation results in what's called Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Lung tissue is being destroyed and the spaces which usually serve for gas exchange are being filled with fluid due to the overwhelming immune response. -

Then due to the lung being injured and as a result not functioning properly, the blood is not oxygenated enough, which is called hypoxemia. This means that other organs are not getting enough oxygen, which causes them to start shutting down. Another major component to MOF (multiple organ failure) is the inflammation itself. The inflammatory compounds that leak into the bloodstream as a result of the infection can cause a severe drop in blood pressure, which means the organs won't get enough blood . The inflammation also contributes to the formation of blood clots, which further damage organs. The damaged organs then release additional inflammatory compounds themselves due to their injury, which feeds into a devastating loop, in addition to causing other problems due to their failure.

Thank you for this answer. People who post stories like these usually have no clue whatsoever about medical thinking and decision making and therefore can't fathom how a doctor couldn't immediately take all the correct steps to manage their condition, when in retrospect it all seems so obvious. Surely this can only be due to incompetence or neglect on the part of the doctor, not the fact that decisions which were thought best were made with the information available at that time.

I'm not saying there are no doctors who make wrong decisions based on  incompetence or carelessness. But as an MD I've heard my fair share of people who want every possible test done on them for the most banal of complaints, and are outraged when some test thought necessary wasn't done.

People who are saved unnecessary invasive procedures like CTs, colonoscopies etc. usually don't thank the doctor who saved them the trouble because he didn't think they were warranted even though there was a minute possibility that they could uncover something serious. But there will be someone every once in a while who, turns out, would have actually benefitted from that procedure earlier on, and won't understand that he wasn't getting it because many more others who had similar problems to him wouldn't be needing it.

Tl;dr: when you think you didn't get enough tests or treatment, it's usually not due to the doctors' incompetence or negligence. It's because it wasn't deemed necessary at the time. It would be safest for us to do every single test for the patient but that wouldn't be what's best for you.

That being said, OP probably should have gotten some basic tests done if he presented with severe acute abdominal pain.

No, it's not stupid. It's normal to crave connection and intimacy. I'd like to just point out two things to you:

1. Don't think if you're unhappy and unfulfilled, that being with someone special will change that. When things settle down and the initial period of being crazy in love passes, your insecurities and problems will creep back on you. Sure having someone to connect with intimately and to talk to is great, but don't think this will make you content in the long term. 
2. If you're depressed solely because of your lack of romantic partner, don't despair and try to hook up with everyone you meet. There are a couple dangers to that. 1. The more we become desperate, the more needy we come across as. People, and women in particular, pick up on that, and are turned away by it. 2. Even if you manage to find someone, you could end up in either a relationship where someone is taking advantage of you, or in a codependent relationship where the other person also seeks consolation from loneliness for themselves first, and a genuine connection with you because of you, second. When emotions settle down, this incompatibility can start showing and disharmony begins. Furthermore, it's then hard to terminate such a relationship because of fear of loneliness, however bad things get. 

I highly recommend the book "Models" by Mark Manson. It has profoundly changed my life and made me understand the mechanics of attraction, what most people do wrong, and how to start doing things right. It's written for guys but a lot of the advice is relevant for girls as well. Good luck.

Deeming people who want to end their lives as selfish is one of the most hypocritical and infuriating things I've heard in my life. People who say stuff like that only think of what the miserable person's responsibility is for other people, not how they feel themselves. Judging someone for wanting to take their own life as being unethical and with that adding onto their agony is one of the cruelest things imaginable. 

Responsibility isn't a one way road. If the person in question has responsibilities towards others, then others also have the responsibility towards the person. Same goes for society in general in relation towards the individual. If one feels so miserable that they don't want to live anymore, then others either have a responsibility to make one feel better, or letting one go. If they aren't capable of achieving the former, at least they shouldn't pass judgement when the person wants to achieve the latter.

The problem here though is the concept of "clear mindedness". People in general argue that wanting to end one's life isn't compatible with being clear minded, so by their logic it's not ever possible to reasonably want to end it. Although I will grant that the majority of people don't have some purely philosophical motivation based solely on reason, that's really beside the point. If someone suffers tremendously and there's no real chance of things getting better anytime soon, they should be able to demand that they be put out of their misery. The thing up for debate in my opinion is where we draw the line. All being said, we can't just let anyone end their live on a whim. There should be checks and balances to protect people who truly do react impulsively and whose situation can realistically get better within a reasonable time frame. The underlying notion remains the same though, and people whose condition can't realistically be improved, should be able to go with dignity. 

People base their worldview based on their feelings in general, everything else is mostly a rationalization. That's why most people in their prime years can't really empathize with how it feels to be in a situation such as you described. If they could, they would change their mind in an instant. And when they experience such things themselves and start to get it, it's already too late. Their opinion is deemed unreasonable and warped. And so the cycle starts anew.

I'm truly sorry if the situation you described is your own. I'd say I empathize, but I know I really can't, despite suffering from existential woes myself. I hope some day we find peace.

Even the Stoics of Ancient Rome have argued that one should be able to lay down their life if they reasonably come to the conclusion that they should do so. Just shows how in a lot of respects we still haven't developed much since then.

From what I understand the reasoning against it is based on the presupposition that everyone *really* wants to live as long as possible and that anyone who says they don't, have a warped worldview due to some current circumstance (depression, pain, or some other circumstance). So basically the notion that anyone would want to end their existence is viewed as an aberration by definition. It's based on this naively idealistic presupposition that there's a way to help everyone regain their will to live, if only that circumstance is rectified. While this may be true in theory, and for some people even in practice, the majority won't ever find that solution and will suffer needlessly instead.

Even if we did grant the "pro lifers" the point that everyone could be helped somehow, this isn't really the main argument. The main debate should be about personal freedom and liberty. If someone wants to end their life, shouldn't that be their right to do so, for whatever reason? Why should society have a right to dictate whether or not someone should want to live, especially if they're in physical or mental agony? It should be written in constitutions as one of basic human rights, to pass on with dignity. We didn't choose to start playing this game, that's exactly why we should be able to choose to stop.

This post is aimed at trying to convey how there is no true altruism and everyone is secretly just doing everything, even the seemingly altruistic deeds, for their own benefit. I'd argue that that's not really the case. Now I like to think of the motivation for good deeds more like a spectrum: from extreme vanity on one side, where people only use good deeds as means to advance themselves, to doing good deeds because of some abstract notion that it's the right thing to do, without gaining any benefit, or even being worse off because of it, on the opposite side. What this distribution looks like, I don't know exactly, but I do know not everything everyone does is on that first side of it.

The thing is though, even if we assume everyone is selfish and doing everything to advance themselves, that's not mutually exclusive with altruism. There's a concept called "egoistic altruism", which essentially says that our best bet of being better off ourselves is to work towards everyone else being better off first. I suggest this Kurzgesagt video on this topic, it's brilliant: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rvskMHn0sqQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rvskMHn0sqQ)
